transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-19
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46m
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Nina Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CascadeOps CTO), Priya Shah (CascadeOps ML Eng), Marco Ruiz (CascadeOps SRE)

[00:00] Jordan Mills: All right, hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll kickoff the week-3 POC lab stitch and fallback playback. Nina and I will run through the numbers then triage routing decisions. Liam, Priya, Marco thanks for making time.

[00:18] Liam O'Connor: Yep thanks, we just wanna see where we stand vs our incumbent and make a call on dedicated slots, so excited to see the numbers.

[00:27] Nina Patel: Cool. Quick agenda: 1) bench readout (512 / 2k token profiles), 2) KV cache impact, 3) routing / fallback playbook, 4) ask / next steps. I'll share screens in a sec.

[00:45] Priya Shah: Quick note, our prod prompt distribution is about 65% short (<256 tokens), 25% mid (256-768), 10% long (>768). we'll attach the histogram after.

[01:02] Nina Patel: Perfect that's exactly what we used for the runs. Ok first slide, baseline provider numbers - note these are from your sample runner against IncumbentCloudAI earlier this month. For 512 tokens: p95 = 340ms, p99 = 980ms, sustained throughput ~18 TPS. For 2048 tokens p95 = 860ms, p99 ~2.4s, throughput drops to ~4 TPS.

[01:35] Marco Ruiz: Those match our internal logs. Their tail is brutal during bursts.

[01:40] Nina Patel: Redwood numbers (same hardware equivalent config, continuous batching disabled for low-latency runs): 512 tokens p95 = 120ms, p99 = 420ms, throughput ~46 TPS. 2048 tokens p95 = 420ms, p99 ~1.1s, throughput ~12 TPS. Cost per token estimate is roughly 0.56x of incumbent under current quantization settings.

[02:10] Liam O'Connor: Wait 46 TPS for 512? that's a big delta. Can you explain config parity?

[02:18] Nina Patel: Yeah - we matched model family, weight quant to BF16 -> we then tried 4-bit quant for the throughput sweep (that's where cost drops). Important callout: for the latency-sensitive runs we also enabled our low-latency kernel selection and per-request routing to low-queue nodes. The bench sheet has exact flags: run_id RK-0319-1, kernels: opt-fuse-v2.

[02:45] Priya Shah: How consistent are p99 numbers? are these single-run OR aggregate?

[02:52] Nina Patel: Aggregate across 3 x 30 minute runs during different load windows; p99 has some variance but the median of medians is around 420ms on 512 tokens. We also measured p95-p99 spread which is tighter than incumbent (less queuing).

[03:12] Jordan Mills: Important pragmatic note: when we enable KV cache for repeated prefixes (your UI prompts reuse system prompt for 40% of calls), compute per token drops by ~48% and tail latencies also drop because there's less compute per request. That was explicit in test RK-0319-3.

[03:33] Priya Shah: That's promising. We have a lot of reuse. Is KV caching safe for PII? we need to make sure prefix caching does not persist sensitive customer content.

[03:42] Nina Patel: Great question — cache is configurable. We can scope it to non-user message prefixes or to session-only caches that flush after 30m. Also it respects token redaction rules and you can opt-out entirely. We documented this in the security note.

[04:00] Marco Ruiz: On the network side we saw some spikes tied to a misconfigured NAT gateway during yesterday's run, I want to confirm we isolate that before the next test.

[04:08] Jordan Mills: Noted - Marco you'll validate VPC egress rules. That was one of today's action items.

[04:15] Nina Patel: Back to routing: we proposed latency-first route -> Redwood hot lane (low-queue dedicated pool) -> if threshold breached route to regional fallback smaller model; for best-effort cost traffic route to default pooling. That gives us an SLO skirt: prioritize p95 during business hours and push cost sensitive loads to batch.

[04:43] Liam O'Connor: Could you expand on fallback? smaller model means quality regressions we need to understand.

[04:50] Nina Patel: Yeah absolutely. Fallback hierarchy we tested: primary is full-quality model (base-13b q4f16 in our run), fallback is base-6b quantized with tuned prompts + response calibration; fallback is invoked only when queue latency > 250ms OR when dedicated slot unavailable. We ran side-by-side evals on 1000 holdout prompts; quality delta was ~3% on our task-specific metric (intent accuracy) with tuned prompt templates. We included example diffs in the bench sheet.

[05:24] Priya Shah: 3% might be tolerable for lowest-priority flows, but not for billing or compliance flows. We'll need strict routing rules by route.

[05:33] Jordan Mills: Totally — Redwood Console supports per-route routing policies and automatic fallback exceptions (you can tag routes as "no-fallback"). We'll set those for billing and legal flows.

[05:45] Marco Ruiz: Any security add'l — are audit logs preserved when we use dedicated slots or private deploy? We need both audit and KMS E2E.

[05:52] Nina Patel: Yes — dedicated and private give you audit logs pushed to your logging sink (S3/Syslog) and you control key wrapping via customer-managed KMS/HSM. We also showed we can rotate keys monthly.

[06:05] Liam O'Connor: Ok good. On the dedicated slot ask — Jordan you mentioned 4 slots? how did you size those?

[06:11] Jordan Mills: We modeled peak concurrency from your telemetry and 4 dedicated GPU-backed slots with autoscale burst gave us peak headroom for 95% of your 9-5 UTC load. Cost estimate is in the deck — rough monthly at current rates $Xk/mo, but I'll send the formal pricing.

[06:30] Priya Shah: Can we try a temporary dedicated slot for the next 72h to observe real traffic?

[06:36] Nina Patel: Yes we can spin up a short-lived reserved capacity for the pilot — we offered that in other pilots, it's done via a trial commit and we capture telemetry into your bench sheet. We just need the network peering info.

[06:48] Marco Ruiz: I'll send peering details and a minimal firewall rule set after the call.

[06:55] Jordan Mills: Great. Back to the bench: we also ran the continuous-batching experiments (to optimize cost under high-load). That increased throughput by ~2.1x for mid tokens but increased p95 by ~60ms; we recommended disabling continuous batching for high-priority low-latency routes.

[07:18] Priya Shah: That matches intuition. For chat features where latency is key we want low-latency kernels; for nightly batch jobs we enable batching.

[07:28] Nina Patel: Exactly. On quantization tradeoffs: our 4-bit runs saved ~44% cost with a small drop in pdf calibration; we used per-layer mixed-precision to preserve quality on attention layers. The bench sheet has side-by-side perplexity and task accuracy numbers.

[07:50] Liam O'Connor: Any weird artifacts or hallucination differences with 4-bit?

[07:56] Nina Patel: On this dataset til now not significant, but we flagged a few edge cases in the longer prompt tests. We'll attach those examples; for safety-critical flows we recommend sticking to 8-bit or fp16.

[08:12] Marco Ruiz: How do fallbacks interact with KV cache? if we fall back to a smaller model do we have to rebuild the cache?

[08:19] Nina Patel: Good point — cache keys are model-aware. A fallback model will miss cache entries for the larger model, but we can configure cross-model cache policies for shared prefixes (with a safety filter). There's a small warmup cost on miss. We included this in the routing playbook.

[08:40] Priya Shah: Can you walk through an example routing decision flow for a single request?

[08:46] Nina Patel: Sure. Example: request arrives -> check route tags (billing=NOFALLBACK, priority=HIGH) -> check queue for hot lane (<2 queued) -> if hot lane OK -> dispatch to low-latency pool with KV cache hit check -> if cache hit return quickly -> if cache miss compute. If hot lane overloaded (>250ms queue) and route allows fallback -> route to fallback model and set telemetry tag flagged_fallback. All events logged.

[09:22] Liam O'Connor: Nice. We'll need the telemetry keys to map flagged_fallback to our downstream analytics.

[09:27] Jordan Mills: We'll provide a telemetry mapping doc.

[09:32] (short silence)

[09:40] Marco Ruiz: On the bench RD traces, can you provide raw per-token timing for 50 sample traces? that's most helpful for our SRE tuning.

[09:48] Nina Patel: Yes, Nina will attach 50 raw traces and end-to-end spans to the bench sheet. Also note that some early traces include NAT retry artifacts (Marco's earlier observation). We'll flag those.

[10:00] Priya Shah: Great. On quality regression monitoring, can Redwood run evals on our weekly upload of prompts? we want automatic alerts if accuracy drifts >2%.

[10:10] Nina Patel: Redwood Optimize can hook up to your evals; we can set regression alerts and tie them to rollout rollback policies. We can demo that next week.

[10:20] Liam O'Connor: Ok, what are the immediate risks you see for production switch?

[10:26] Nina Patel: Biggest risks: 1) network egress misconfig (we already saw a NAT spike), 2) noisy neighbors if dedicated capacity under-provisioned, 3) model calibration drift if we use aggressive quant. Mitigations: VPC peering validation, short dedicated trial, conservative quant for safety flows.

[10:44] Jordan Mills: We've added a fallback playbook that automatically scales up hot lane capacity before falling back, to reduce quality regressions. Also we have scheduled canary ramp with auto rollback.

[10:55] Marco Ruiz: How does the canary rollback trigger work? is it latency or quality based?

[11:02] Nina Patel: Both. You configure signal thresholds: latency p95>threshold or eval accuracy drop >X triggers an automatic rollback to previous model or route. You can also do manual rollbacks.

[11:18] Priya Shah: I want to see an example of the rollback timeline and a sample alert.

[11:23] Jordan Mills: We'll include screenshot examples in the follow up deck.

[11:28] (pause)

[11:35] Liam O'Connor: Ok last thing on cost — can you show a side-by-side monthly cost projection assuming 100M tokens/month under our distribution?

[11:43] Nina Patel: Yes, we provided three scenarios in the sheet: conservative (no quant, no cache), baseline (q4 + partial cache), aggressive (q4 + full cache + batching). For baseline we estimate ~0.56x incumbent; with aggressive configs it can be ~0.35x. Jordan will share the sheet and call out the assumptions.

[12:05] Jordan Mills: I'll call out assumptions: token mix, model selection, slot count, and expected uptime. We'll annotate cells so you can tweak.

[12:18] Priya Shah: Sounds good. If we do a 72h dedicated trial can we enable KV cache selectively to observe real-world improvement?

[12:25] Nina Patel: Absolutely. We recommend doing a staged approach: day 1 no cache, day 2 cache-on for non-PII routes, day 3 full config. That lets you measure delta and any unexpected behavior.

[12:40] Marco Ruiz: Agreed. I'll coordinate firewall and peering and we can start as soon as that's done.

[12:47] Jordan Mills: OK to recap and next steps: 1) Nina to run 10k KV-cache run and attach traces (due 3/22), 2) Marco to confirm VPC peering/rules (due 3/23), 3) Jordan to send dedicated slot pricing (due 3/24) and deck links (done). Any other items?

[13:05] Liam O'Connor: Please also include example telemetry keys and the rollback sample in the follow-up.

[13:12] Jordan Mills: Will do. Anything else?

[13:16] Priya Shah: No, that's it. Thanks team.

[13:20] (meeting closes, small chatter)

Notes on transcript quality: automatic transcription had a few mis-heard acronyms (we saw "KV cash" once, and model name fused as "base-thirteen bee"), timestamps approximate.
